paper_metadata.title: Doc‐KG: Unstructured documents to knowledge graph construction, identification and validation with Wikidata
paper_metadata.abstract: The paper introduces Doc-KG, a system that transforms unstructured documents into structured knowledge by extracting local RDF triples and mapping them to a target knowledge graph such as Wikidata. It uses syntactic information to extract entities and predicates, constructs local knowledge graphs, and identifies corresponding Wikidata URIs. Evaluation on WebNLG reports 86.64% accuracy for triple extraction and 61.35% mapping of the local KG to Wikidata, with 38.65% described as novel information. A manually annotated qualitative evaluation reports better triple extraction than the baselines.

problem_addressed: The paper addresses automatic construction and enrichment of knowledge graphs from unstructured natural-language documents, focusing on extracting subject-predicate-object triples and identifying or mapping those triples in Wikidata. It motivates the work by noting the lack of a standard benchmark for triple extraction from unstructured text and the limited prior work on mapping extracted triples to Wikidata.

methodology.description: Doc-KG is a sequential classical-NLP pipeline. It tokenizes, sentence-splits, lemmatizes, POS-tags, and syntactically parses input text. Dependency labels identify subject and object tokens, while ROOT, AMOD, ADJ, AGENT, and ATTR labels identify predicate tokens. The resulting subject-predicate-object triples are appended to a schema-free local KG. Entity mentions are mapped to Wikidata through exact-label SPARQL queries, with predefined Wikidata URIs for typed values such as dates, numbers, percentages, and money. Predicates are mapped using a locally indexed list of Wikidata properties and alternative labels, followed by stop-word cleaning. The system is compared with SpaCy/Textacy SVO and Stanford CoreNLP OpenIE.

ontology_or_schema_use.value: The extraction stage is schema-free and stores textual SPO triples. The linking stage uses Wikidata as the target KG and its RDF/URI vocabulary: entity labels are queried through SPARQL, predicates are matched against Wikidata base properties and alternative labels, and typed values receive predefined Wikidata URIs. The paper also suggests future use of domain-specific ontologies.

text_to_kg_stages: Text preprocessing: tokenization, sentence segmentation, lemmatization, stop-word removal, n-gram modelling, and sentence cleaning
Entity and concept extraction: dependency-based subject and object extraction
Entity typing: predefined handling of numerical, date, percentage, time, and monetary values
Entity resolution and linking: exact-label matching and Wikidata URI assignment
Relation and triple extraction: dependency-based predicate extraction and SPO formation
Graph construction: appending extracted triples to a schema-free local KG
Knowledge fusion and deduplication: mapping local triples to Wikidata properties, alternative labels, and URIs
Graph validation and correction: qualitative comparison with Wikidata and manually annotated ground truth

input_output.input_type: Unstructured natural-language text, including raw document sentences; evaluation inputs are sentences derived from WebNLG's 1-Triple-to-Text corpus and Wikipedia sentences for TinyButMighty.
input_output.input_granularity: Sentence-level processing; each sentence is processed independently in the extraction algorithm, with the quantitative WebNLG setup targeting one triple per sentence.
input_output.output_representation: A local schema-free knowledge graph represented as subject-predicate-object textual triples, followed by an annotated/mapped KG whose entities and predicates may be assigned Wikidata URIs or newly created URIs.

models_and_tools: Local Wikidata predicate index with base and alternative labels
Custom triple-set precision, recall, and F-measure evaluation algorithm
datasets: WebNLG-derived quantitative dataset: 7,686 sentences across 16 domains, including Airports, Artists, Astronauts, Athletes, Buildings, Celestial Body, Cities, Cosmic Characters, Companies, Foods, Transportation Means, Monuments, Politicians, Sports Teams, Universities, and Books Writers
Manually annotated WebNLG sample: 80 sentences and 326 triples, as described in the dataset section
TinyButMighty crowdsourced/Wikipedia dataset: 80 compound and complex sentences with 327 annotations; the results section refers to 326 ground-truth triples
Wikidata, used as the external target knowledge graph for entity and predicate identification

metrics: Quantitative sentence-level extraction accuracy: extracted triples divided by total sentences
Wikidata mapping percentages for subjects, predicates, objects, complete triples, and triples including typed entities
Cosine similarity and Jaccard similarity for extracted versus annotated triple sets
Similarity-threshold F-measure with penalty below 0.50 and amnesty above 0.75
Precision, recall, and F-measure computed using the custom triple-set algorithm
baselines: SpaCy/Textacy SVO on cleaned text with stop-word removal
evaluation.setting: Quantitative evaluation uses 7,686 WebNLG-derived sentences and aims to extract one triple per sentence. Qualitative evaluation uses Wikidata endpoint matching and manually annotated sentences. Baselines are evaluated on the same extraction datasets; the custom qualitative metric compares generated triples with human annotations using textual similarity, thresholds, cosine/Jaccard coefficients, and aggregated precision, recall, and F-measure. A domain-specific comparison is also shown for CoreNLP OpenIE and Doc-KG.

value: Doc-KG extracted 6,659 triples with 86.64% quantitative accuracy on 7,686 WebNLG-derived sentences, compared with 69.45% for Stanford CoreNLP, 7.43% for SpaCy SVO, and 33.11% for cleaned-text SpaCy SVO.

In external Wikidata mapping, the paper reports identification of 67.66% of subjects, 78.19% of predicates, and 71.75% of objects; complete triple mapping was 21.89%, increasing to 61.35% when typed entities were included.

On the manually annotated qualitative sample, Doc-KG identified 310 triples, while OpenIE identified 834 and SpaCy identified 59. The reported overall qualitative scores with penalty and amnesty were 38.15% for Doc-KG, 31.19% for OpenIE, and 2.71% for SpaCy.

On the custom standard-metric evaluation, Doc-KG achieved recall 97.86%, precision 44.68%, and F-measure 61.35%; OpenIE achieved 39.16%, 55.57%, and 45.94%, while SpaCy achieved 11.31%, 12.54%, and 11.90%, respectively.
The paper reports that OpenIE outperformed Doc-KG in the Astronauts and Athletes domains, while performance was comparable for Artists.

value: Paper-reported strength: the dependency-based method achieved the highest quantitative extraction accuracy among the evaluated systems on the WebNLG-derived dataset.
Paper-reported strength: typed-entity URI handling substantially increased the proportion of local triples identified in Wikidata from 21.89% completely mapped triples to 61.35%.
Paper-reported strength: the method has a simple pipeline and does not require extensive preprocessing or entity disambiguation while still producing promising extraction results.
Review-level inference: the explicit separation of local triple construction from target-KG mapping makes the workflow relatively interpretable and auditable.

incorporating typed subjects and objects significantly increased the number of identified triples to 61.35%.
Despite not employing extensive pre-processing and entity disambiguation techniques, our system demonstrated efficient performance.

value: Paper-reported weakness: SpaCy SVO performs poorly on complex sentence structures and improves markedly only after stop-word removal.
Paper-reported weakness: Stanford OpenIE can generate non-informative triples such as [Mark Zuckerberg, is, CEO].

Paper-reported weakness: predicate mapping is difficult because natural-language predicates can use different words for similar concepts; the proposed method relies on exact or alternative-label string matching after cleaning.
Review-level inference: the 44.68% precision reported for Doc-KG is lower than OpenIE's 55.57%, indicating a substantial false-positive trade-off despite high recall.
Review-level inference: the method's exact-label matching and newly created URIs may be brittle for aliases, ambiguity, paraphrases, and entities absent from Wikidata.

value: The paper leaves unresolved robust triple extraction from complex and diverse unstructured sentences.
Entity disambiguation and linking remain unresolved when multiple Wikidata entities have similar labels or when exact labels are unavailable.
Predicate normalization remains difficult for paraphrases and semantically equivalent natural-language relations.
The lack of a standardized benchmark for triple extraction and KG validation remains unresolved.
The precision-recall trade-off remains unresolved: Doc-KG obtains very high recall but lower precision than OpenIE in the reported qualitative evaluation.
The paper identifies future but unresolved integration of semantic role labeling, domain ontologies, and LLM-based extraction.
